Credits.intro: A tool is never born alone. Here are the people who, closely or from a distance, had a hand in making it.
Credits.familyBody: It all starts there. Julien — my brother, Piza — whose musical ear and sense of theory are in every measure of this tool. My father, who put guitars in our hands before we knew what to do with them. My mother, who has since picked up guitar and bass herself — because once music gets into a house, it never really leaves.
Credits.bandBody: The people it all really started with — the first rehearsals in garages and at the youth club, the first gigs, the first riffs learned together. Alviena exists a little bit for them, and because of them.
Credits.gregBody: A brilliant guitarist and a man of vision. Greg was one of the first to understand what this tool could become, to help shape it with me, and to ask the right questions at the right time. The kind of outside perspective that changes everything.
Credits.bastienBody: A guitarist and a developer — the dream combination for this project. Bastien understands both sides of it: what a musician expects from a tool, and how to build it properly. His help means a lot.
Credits.closing: And to everyone who uses Alviena, shares their chord sheets, and sends feedback — thank you. You're the best reason to keep going.

Faq.pageSubtitle: Everything you need to get started with Alviena.
Faq.s1a1: Alviena is a web app for creating, organizing, and sharing chord sheets. You can enter your sheets by hand, import them from chord text, or extract them automatically from a photo of sheet music. Sheets are accessible from any device, and you can print them or use them live on stage without installing anything.
Faq.s1q2: How do I create a sheet?
Faq.s1a2: From the dashboard or the "+ Sheet" button at the top right, you have three options: start from a blank sheet and enter chords by hand, paste text in chord+lyrics format, or drop in a photo of sheet music for automatic AI transcription.
Faq.s2q1: How do I import a sheet from text?
Faq.s2a1: Copy the text of a sheet in chord+lyrics format (chords written above the lyrics, sections named like [Verse] or [Chorus]), then in Alviena click "+ Sheet" → "Import text" and paste it in. The app automatically detects the title, artist, key, tempo, and section structure.
Faq.s2q2: How does sheet music analysis work?
Faq.s2a2: You upload one or more photos of your sheet music (JPG, PNG, WebP). An AI model analyzes the images, identifies chords measure by measure, the song structure (intro, verse, chorus…), repeats, and the time signature, then automatically generates a sheet. You can then correct it in the editor.
Faq.s2q3: The detected chords are wrong, what should I do?
Faq.s2a3: Text import and sheet music analysis are automatic interpretations — the AI does its best but can make mistakes, especially with durations, complex chords, or ambiguous passages. That's completely normal. In the editor, you can correct or override any chord however you like: change the name, extend or split the duration, add or remove cells. The sheet is yours.
Faq.s3a1: Yes. In the editor, you can define your own fingerings for chords that aren't in the library, or modify an existing fingering. These custom chords are saved with the sheet and shown in the diagrams.
Faq.s3a2: Alviena supports seven instruments: Guitar, Ukulele, Mandolin, Banjo, Bass, Piano, and Voice. Each instrument has its own chord library and diagrams (fretboard or keyboard depending on the instrument).
Faq.s3q3: Is French notation (Do Ré Mi) supported?
Faq.s3a3: Yes. In your profile, you can choose between American notation (C D E F G A B) and French notation (Do Ré Mi Fa Sol La Si). The display switches across the whole app, while chords remain stored in American notation.
Faq.s4q1: Are my sheets visible to everyone?
Faq.s4a1: No, all sheets are private by default. You can make them public from the editor (they then appear on the Explore page), or share them via a unique link without making them public ("unlisted" mode).
Faq.s4a2: A Group lets you share sheets with other musicians. The creator invites members via a link, and sheets linked to the group are accessible to all members, even if they're private. Handy for a band or a class.
Faq.s4a3: A Set is a setlist: an ordered list of sheets for a gig or rehearsal. In concert mode ("Play"), sheets scroll through in full screen, chords are enlarged, and you move from one song to the next with a swipe or a click.
Faq.s4q4: What's the difference between a Set and a Group?
Faq.s4a4: A Set is a personal planning tool: you put songs in order for a gig or rehearsal, and play them in full-screen mode. A Group is a shared space: it brings musicians together and gives them access to the same sheets. The two are complementary — you can build a Set from sheets shared in your Group.
Faq.s5q1: How do I transpose a sheet?
Faq.s5a1: In viewing mode, a transpose selector is available at the bottom of the screen. You can shift from −6 to +6 semitones in real time. Transposition is just a display setting: the original sheet is kept as is.
Faq.s5a2: Yes. A print button is available in viewing mode. The layout adapts automatically for a clean printout: the navbar and controls disappear, and chord diagrams can optionally be included.

ChordDetect.h1: Identify a chord with your microphone
ChordDetect.intro: Play a chord: the microphone listens and the detected chord appears live, along with the closest candidates.
ChordDetect.footnote: Recognises 12 families: maj, min, 7, m7, maj7, 6, m6, sus2, sus4, dim, aug, m7b5. American notation. Note: chords made of the same notes cannot be told apart (e.g. C6 = Am7).

About.lead: A story of family, strings, and memory.
About.p1: Our father is a guitarist. We grew up with guitars lying around in corners, chords drifting out of a room, a house where music was a language of its own. For Alexandre, it really took hold at thirteen — that feeling of putting your fingers on a neck and sensing something fall into place. His younger brother Julien went for the drums. Two and a half years apart, two different approaches, one shared playground.
About.p2: At fifteen or sixteen we started our first band. We knew very little but we played gigs, fell flat, started again. We spent hours on forums, on Guitar Pro, working out tablature, swapping things found late at night. Music became our way of getting together — birthdays, Christmas, weekends: so many chances to ask for another instrument. A bass. A ukulele. A piano. A banjo, a mandolin, a pan flute, a melodica, castanets. We tried everything, from metal to classical, with no hierarchy and no borders.
About.p3: Twenty years have gone by. We are thirty-five now, and we still play together — with more maturity, a better ear, more experience. Yet the struggle is strangely unchanged: what were the chords again? What is the structure? What order do we play it in? And with it a quiet frustration: all those songs learnt twenty years ago, those riffs, those progressions, those arrangements — gone. Lost somewhere between two house moves and a hard drive upgrade.
About.p4: Alviena came out of that. Out of a simple, slightly painful need: not to lose what we had learnt. To remember. To have somewhere to write a chart down properly, to find a chord at two in the morning before a rehearsal, to share the structure of a song without sending a blurry photo of a spiral notebook.
About.p5: We built it together. Alexandre on the technical side, Julien — known as Piza — on the musical vision, the theory, the rigour of someone who genuinely reads a score. What one of us cannot do, the other carries. That has been how we work from the start.
About.p6: Building the tool, we realised it was not only for us. A band in rehearsal needs one shared reading — not five different versions of the same song on five phones. A guitar teacher needs to hand charts to a class without it turning into a puzzle. A musician on their own needs a book, a repertoire, something personal that lasts.
About.p7: Alviena handles many instruments because we do. It is built for playing together because that is the only reason we started. And it looks ahead — AI to transcribe a score, organising a gig, sharing within a band — because we now have the technical means to solve problems we have been carrying since our teens.
About.closing: It is a tool made by musicians, for musicians. No more, no less.
